PSE II · Chapter 24

Electric Potential

Energy, voltage & the scalar view of fields

← PSE II Course

24.0 — Energy Joins the Story

Chapter 22 asked how strong — and answered with a vector at every point in space. Chapter 23 asked how much charge — and answered by counting field lines through a closed surface. Both answers are vectors or fluxes: objects with direction, or objects that need a surface before they mean anything.

This chapter asks a third question — how much work — and the answer is a single number at every point. No components. No direction. One number.

That is not a small convenience. In Physics I you learned that energy methods often beat force methods: instead of tracking forces and accelerations through a complicated path, you relate the initial and final states directly and let the path take care of itself. The same trade is available here, and for the same reason: the electric force is conservative.

The concept is also the one you already use without naming. A “12-volt battery,” a “120-volt outlet” — these are statements about potential difference. The volt, named for Alessandro Volta (1745–1827), is the unit we are about to define properly.

“The language of experiment is more authoritative than any reasoning: facts can destroy our ratiocination — not vice versa.” — Alessandro Volta

The quantity instruments actually read

There is a practical reason this chapter matters as much as a conceptual one. No instrument measures an electric field directly. A voltmeter has two leads and returns one number: the potential difference between them. Field-mapping apparatus works the same way — a probe reads potential at a point, and the field is reconstructed afterwards from how that reading varies across the region.

So potential is not merely a convenient scalar stand-in for the field. It is the thing laboratory work produces, and the field is the thing inferred from it. §24.3 and §24.5 supply the two halves of that inference.

The Gravitational Analogy

Every result in this chapter has a gravitational twin you already know. The analogy is not decoration — it is the fastest available check on whether a result is sensible.

Gravitational system Electrical system
Gravitational field \(\vec{g}\) Electric field \(\vec{E}\)
Mass \(m\) feels \(\vec{F} = m\vec{g}\) Charge \(q\) feels \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\)
Potential energy \(U_g = mgh\) Potential energy \(U_E\)
Potential \(V_g = gh = U_g/m\) Potential \(V = U_E/q\)
\(\vec{g} = -\nabla V_g\) \(\vec{E} = -\nabla V\)

Just as gravitational potential \(gh\) is potential energy per unit mass, electric potential \(V\) is potential energy per unit charge. The one place the analogy breaks is sign: gravity only attracts, so \(U_g\) is always negative, while charges do both.

24.1 — Electric Potential Energy

Why potential energy exists at all

Potential energy is only definable for a conservative force — one whose work depends on the endpoints and not on the path. The electric force qualifies for the same reason gravity does: it is central and depends only on position. Take any closed path in an electrostatic field and the net work is zero.

That fact is what licenses everything below. If the work depended on the route, “the potential energy at point P” would not be a number, and there would be no chapter.

Potential Energy in a Uniform Field

Take a uniform field \(\vec{E}\) and move a charge \(q\) through a displacement \(\vec{d}\). The force is constant, so the work done by the field is

\[W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = q\vec{E}\cdot\vec{d}\]

and for motion straight along the field, \(W = qEd\). The change in potential energy is defined as the negative of that work:

\[\boxed{\;\Delta U_E = -W = -qEd\;}\]

Does the sign behave? Release a positive charge in a field. It accelerates along \(\vec{E}\), the field does positive work, and \(\Delta U_E\) is negative — potential energy falls, kinetic energy rises. That is a ball rolling downhill, and it should feel identical, because \(-qEd\) and \(-mgh\) are the same statement with the same structure.

Now release a negative charge in the same field. It accelerates against \(\vec{E}\). The field still does positive work on it and \(U_E\) still falls — but “downhill” now points the other way. Potential energy always decreases along the direction the particle actually moves; it is the direction that flips, not the energy bookkeeping.

Potential Energy of a Pair of Point Charges

For two point charges separated by \(r\), integrating the work needed to bring one in from infinity against the other’s Coulomb force gives

\[\boxed{\;U_E = k_e\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}\;}\]

Three features carry the physics:

  • Same sign → \(U_E > 0\). You had to do work to push them together, and that work is stored, waiting to be released if you let go.
  • Opposite signs → \(U_E < 0\). They pulled themselves together; you would have to do work to separate them.
  • \(U_E \rightarrow 0\) as \(r \rightarrow \infty\). This is a choice of reference, not a derived fact. Infinity is convenient because it makes \(U_E\) measure “the work to assemble this from scattered pieces.”

Note the exponent. The force between two charges goes as \(1/r^2\); the energy goes as \(1/r\). The energy is the integral of the force over distance, so it must carry one fewer power of \(r\). Any time you see those two exponents together, that is the relationship you are looking at.

Against the gravitational case

Gravitational Electric
Expression \(U_g = -G\dfrac{m_1m_2}{r}\) \(U_E = k_e\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r}\)
Sign always negative either sign
Reference \(U_g = 0\) at \(r = \infty\) \(U_E = 0\) at \(r = \infty\)

The explicit minus sign in the gravitational form is doing the work that the charges’ signs do in the electric form. Masses only attract, so the sign is baked in; charges do both, so it is carried by \(q_1q_2\).

Systems of More Than Two Charges

Potential energy belongs to a system, not to a particle. For several charges, total up every pair exactly once:

\[\boxed{\;U_E = k_e\sum_{i<j}\frac{q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}\;}\]

For three charges that is

\[U_E = k_e\left(\frac{q_1q_2}{r_{12}} + \frac{q_1q_3}{r_{13}} + \frac{q_2q_3}{r_{23}}\right)\]

The \(i<j\) condition is not bookkeeping fussiness. Writing \(q_1q_2/r_{12}\) and \(q_2q_1/r_{21}\) counts the same physical interaction twice and doubles the answer. Three charges have three pairs, four charges have six, five have ten — the count is \(\binom{n}{2}\), and it grows faster than the number of charges.

Putting Numbers on It

Three charges sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side \(a = 0.30\ \text{m}\): \(q_1 = +2.0\ \mu\text{C}\), \(q_2 = +2.0\ \mu\text{C}\), \(q_3 = -3.0\ \mu\text{C}\). Every separation is the same \(a\), so the geometry factors out and only the charge products differ.

Pair \(q_iq_j\) (\(\mu\text{C}^2\)) \(U\) (J)
1–2 \(+4.0\) \(+0.120\)
1–3 \(-6.0\) \(-0.180\)
2–3 \(-6.0\) \(-0.180\)
total \(\mathbf{-0.240}\)

The total is negative, and that is the whole story of the configuration: the two attractive pairs outweigh the single repulsive one. Negative assembly energy means the system is bound — it took net negative work to build, so you would have to supply \(+0.240\) J to scatter these three back to infinity.

Change \(q_3\) to \(+3.0\ \mu\text{C}\) and every term flips positive, giving \(+0.480\) J: the same geometry, now an unbound configuration that will fly apart the instant it is released. The sign of \(U_E\) is a stability statement, not a bookkeeping detail.

24.2 — Electric Potential

Dividing out the test charge

In Chapter 22 we did not stop at the force between two charges — we divided by the test charge to get a field, \(\vec{E} = \vec{F}/q\), which describes what the source does to space regardless of what you put there. Do the same thing to energy:

\[\boxed{\;V = \frac{U_E}{q}\;}\]

The potential difference between two points is what you almost always actually use:

\[\Delta V = V_B - V_A = \frac{\Delta U_E}{q} = -\frac{W_{A\rightarrow B}}{q}\]

This is the single most important move in the chapter. \(U_E\) needs two objects — the source and the charge you brought. \(V\) needs only the source. It is a property of the space, sitting there whether or not anyone comes to measure it.

The Volt

\[1\ \text{V} = 1\ \frac{\text{J}}{\text{C}}\]

One volt is one joule of potential energy for every coulomb of charge you place there. A 12 V battery does 12 joules of work on every coulomb it drives around the circuit.

The unit identity that is secretly a physical law. Since \(1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}\),

\[1\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{C}} = 1\ \frac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}\]

Read the right-hand side as volts per meter. The electric field is the rate at which potential changes with position. That is not a unit conversion — it is the whole content of §24.5 arriving three sections early, hidden inside a dimensional check. If the field is strong, the potential is falling steeply; if the potential is flat, there is no field.

This is why dimensional analysis is not a formality. The units of a quantity frequently tell you what it is.

The Electron Volt

The joule is absurdly oversized for one particle. Define the electron volt as the energy one elementary charge gains crossing one volt:

\[1\ \text{eV} = \left(1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}\right)\left(1\ \text{V}\right) = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}\]

Process Energy scale
Visible-light photon 1.8–3.1 eV
Chemical bond ~1–10 eV
Medical X-ray ~10–100 keV
Nuclear binding ~1–10 MeV

The eV is not a new physical idea — it is a unit chosen so the numbers you write down are of order one. Notice that the table spans six orders of magnitude, and that chemistry and visible light sit at the same scale. That is not a coincidence: chemistry is the physics of a few eV.

Potential versus Potential Energy

These are confused constantly, and the confusion is expensive. Keep them apart:

Electric potential \(V\) Electric potential energy \(U_E\)
Belongs to the field, i.e. the source charges the system: source and test charge
Exists without a test charge? yes no
Units volts (J/C) joules
Relation \(V = U_E/q\) \(U_E = qV\)

The analogy that works: potential is height. A point on a hillside has a definite height whether or not anyone is standing there. Gravitational potential energy needs both the height and a hiker.

24.3 — Potential Difference in a Uniform Field

The general relation, and the uniform case

For any field, potential difference is the line integral of the field:

\[\boxed{\;V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}\;}\]

If the field is uniform and the path runs straight along it, \(\vec{E}\) comes out of the integral and this collapses to

\[\Delta V = -Ed\]

where \(d\) is the displacement along the field direction.

Which way does potential decrease? The minus sign says: moving along \(\vec{E}\), potential drops. Field lines point downhill.

Two consequences worth holding onto:

  • A positive charge released from rest moves toward lower potential — it falls downhill, like a ball.
  • A negative charge released from rest moves toward higher potential — it falls uphill in potential, because for it \(U_E = qV\) decreases as \(V\) rises.

Both are the same statement: every charge moves so as to reduce its own potential energy. Only the map from \(V\) to \(U_E\) carries the sign.

Equipotential Surfaces

An equipotential surface is a surface on which \(V\) is constant. Four properties, and each one is derivable rather than memorisable:

  1. No work is done moving a charge along one. \(\Delta V = 0\), so \(W = -q\Delta V = 0\).
  2. They are perpendicular to field lines, everywhere. If \(\vec{E}\) had any component along the surface, moving a charge that way would do work — which property 1 forbids. So the field must be entirely perpendicular.
  3. They never cross. A crossing point would have two different potentials.
  4. Their spacing measures field strength. Closely packed equipotentials mean \(V\) changes rapidly with position, and by §24.2’s unit identity that is a strong field.

How a field is mapped in practice

Properties 1 and 2 together are the basis of every experimental field map. A probe reads potential, so what it traces are curves of constant reading — equipotentials, by property 1. No field line is ever measured.

Property 2 then supplies the field for nothing: draw the equipotentials, draw perpendiculars to them, and those perpendiculars are the field lines. Their spacing, by property 4, gives the magnitude. The measurement yields a scalar and geometry converts it into a vector field — which is the practical answer to why potential is worth defining at all.

Rule 5 of Chapter 22 — field lines meet a conductor’s surface at right angles — is the same statement in a special case, because a conductor’s surface is an equipotential (§24.7).

Uniform Field Equipotentials

In a uniform field the equipotentials are parallel planes perpendicular to \(\vec{E}\), evenly spaced — even spacing being the geometric signature of a constant field. Between capacitor plates held at potential difference \(\Delta V\) and separation \(d\):

\[E = \frac{\Delta V}{d}\]

Putting Numbers on It

A 12 V battery across plates \(d = 0.30\ \text{cm} = 3.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}\) apart:

\[E = \frac{12\ \text{V}}{3.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}} = 4.0\times10^{3}\ \text{V/m}\]

Is that a lot? Dry air breaks down at about \(3\times10^{6}\ \text{V/m}\), so this is roughly a factor of 750 below sparking — safe, and nowhere near the limit.

Now run it backwards. To reach breakdown with the same 12 V battery you would need \(d = 12/(3\times10^6) = 4\ \mu\text{m}\): a gap about a twentieth the width of a human hair. Ordinary voltages make extraordinary fields once the gap gets small enough, which is the entire operating principle of every microelectronic device you own, and the reason they fail when a dust particle bridges a gap.

A Charge Released from Rest

Because the electric force is conservative, mechanical energy is conserved, and the whole apparatus of Physics I applies unchanged:

\[\boxed{\;K_i + qV_i = K_f + qV_f\;}\]

Equivalently \(\Delta K = -q\Delta V\). This is the fastest route to any “released from rest, how fast is it going” question, and it never requires you to find the acceleration or the time.

A proton across 100 V

A proton starts at rest at the positive plate of a capacitor with \(\Delta V = 100\ \text{V}\) and crosses to the negative plate.

Starting from \(K_i + qV_i = K_f + qV_f\) with \(K_i = 0\):

\[q\left(V_i - V_f\right) = \tfrac12 mv_f^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_f = \sqrt{\frac{2q\,\Delta V}{m}}\]

\[v_f = \sqrt{\frac{2\left(1.602\times10^{-19}\right)\left(100\right)}{1.673\times10^{-27}}} = 1.38\times10^{5}\ \text{m/s}\]

Three checks, all cheap.

  • Dimensions. \(\sqrt{\text{C}\cdot\text{V}/\text{kg}} = \sqrt{\text{J}/\text{kg}} = \text{m/s}\). ✓
  • Scaling. \(v_f \propto \sqrt{\Delta V}\) — quadrupling the voltage only doubles the speed. Energy is what the voltage buys, and speed is the square root of energy.
  • Magnitude. \(1.38\times10^{5}\) m/s is about 0.05% of light speed, so non-relativistic treatment was justified. Had we used an electron, the same 100 V would give \(5.9\times10^{6}\) m/s — 1836 times lighter, so \(\sqrt{1836} \approx 43\) times faster. Still safe, but you can see how quickly electrons get fast, which is why the eV exists as a unit.

24.4 — Electric Potential Due to Point Charges

The potential of a single point charge

Start from the definition and integrate in from infinity along a radial path, where \(\vec{E} = k_e q/r^2\,\hat{r}\) is parallel to \(d\vec{s}\):

\[V = -\int_\infty^r k_e\frac{q}{r'^2}\,dr' = k_e q\left[\frac{1}{r'}\right]_\infty^r\]

\[\boxed{\;V = k_e\frac{q}{r}\;}\]

  • \(V > 0\) around a positive charge — a potential hill.
  • \(V < 0\) around a negative charge — a potential well.
  • \(V \rightarrow 0\) as \(r \rightarrow \infty\), matching the reference chosen in §24.1.
  • \(V \rightarrow \pm\infty\) as \(r \rightarrow 0\). The divergence is an artefact of the point-charge idealization; real charge distributions have finite size.

Why \(1/r\) when the field goes as \(1/r^2\)?

Because potential is the integral of field over distance, and integrating \(r^{-2}\) gives \(r^{-1}\). One power of \(r\) is spent in the integration.

This is worth more than it looks. It means potential falls off more slowly than field, so a charge distribution’s influence on potential reaches further than its influence on field. It also gives you a free consistency test on anything you derive: if you find a potential going as \(1/r^2\), the field it came from had better go as \(1/r^3\) — as it does for a dipole, below.

Superposition — and why this is the payoff

Potential is a scalar. For several charges, add the numbers:

\[\boxed{\;V = k_e\sum_i \frac{q_i}{r_i}\;}\]

Compare this with what Chapter 22 cost

In Chapter 22 you found the field of two charges on the \(y\)-axis. That required: resolving each contribution into components, tracking two signs and two directions, finding a common denominator, and recombining. The result filled a line and needed care at every step.

The potential of the same two charges is \(k_e q_1/r_1 + k_e q_2/r_2\). Two divisions and an addition. No components, no directions, no unit vectors.

This is the trade the chapter is built on. You give up direction information in exchange for arithmetic that is a fraction of the work — and §24.5 shows you can get the direction back whenever you want it, by differentiating. Potential is not a different physics; it is the same physics stored in a cheaper format.

Putting Numbers on It

\(q_1 = +3.0\ \mu\text{C}\) sits at the origin; \(q_2 = -1.0\ \mu\text{C}\) sits at \(x = 0.40\ \text{m}\). Find \(V\) at point A on the \(x\)-axis at \(x = 0.20\) m, and at point B at \(x = 0.60\) m.

\(r_1\) (m) \(r_2\) (m) \(k_eq_1/r_1\) (V) \(k_eq_2/r_2\) (V) \(V\) (V)
A (\(x=0.20\)) 0.20 0.20 \(+1.35\times10^{5}\) \(-4.49\times10^{4}\) \(+8.99\times10^{4}\)
B (\(x=0.60\)) 0.60 0.20 \(+4.49\times10^{4}\) \(-4.49\times10^{4}\) \(\mathbf{0}\)

\[\Delta V = V_B - V_A = -8.99\times10^{4}\ \text{V}\]

Two things to notice, and the second is the important one.

At B the potential is exactly zero — because B is three times as far from the \(+3\ \mu\)C as from the \(-1\ \mu\)C, and the charge ratio is exactly 3. Whenever \(|q_1|/r_1 = |q_2|/r_2\) for opposite signs, the contributions cancel.

But the field at B is not zero. Potential is a scalar and the two contributions cancelled as numbers; the two field vectors at B both point in the \(+x\) direction and add. \(V = 0\) does not mean \(E = 0\), and confusing the two is the single most common error in this chapter. A zero of potential is a statement about the work to bring a charge in from infinity — and there are paths in from infinity along which the work done in one region is undone in another.

Worked Case: The Electric Dipole

A dipole is \(+q\) and \(-q\) separated by \(2a\), centered at the origin on the \(x\)-axis.

On the perpendicular bisector (the \(y\)-axis, height \(y\)), both charges are the same distance \(r = \sqrt{a^2+y^2}\) away, so

\[V = k_e\frac{+q}{r} + k_e\frac{-q}{r} = 0\]

The potential vanishes on the entire bisecting plane — for any \(y\), near or far. It is exactly the situation of point B above, made into a whole surface.

On the axis at \(x > a\):

\[V = k_e q\left(\frac{1}{x-a} - \frac{1}{x+a}\right) = k_e q\,\frac{2a}{x^2-a^2}\]

Far from the dipole, \(x \gg a\), so \(x^2 - a^2 \rightarrow x^2\) and

\[V \approx \frac{2k_e qa}{x^2} = \frac{k_e p}{x^2},\qquad p \equiv 2qa\]

The potential of a dipole falls as \(1/r^2\) — faster than a point charge’s \(1/r\). It must: from far away the dipole is electrically neutral, so its leading \(1/r\) term has to cancel, leaving the next one.

Cross-check it against §24.4’s rule. If \(V \sim 1/r^2\), then \(E = -dV/dr \sim 1/r^3\) — which is exactly the dipole field you found in Chapter 22 with vectors and a great deal more effort. Same answer, one derivative, no components.

24.5 — Obtaining the Electric Field from the Potential

The gradient relationship

Potential difference is the integral of field. Run it backwards and the field is the derivative of potential:

\[\boxed{\;\vec{E} = -\nabla V = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)\;}\]

In one dimension, \(E_x = -dV/dx\).

The field points in the direction of steepest decrease of potential, with magnitude equal to that rate of decrease. Reading a \(V\)-versus-\(x\) graph: the slope gives \(-E_x\), steep means strong, flat means zero.

The three components are independent partial derivatives. This is why one scalar function can carry a three-component vector field: the direction information was never lost, only folded into how \(V\) varies from place to place.

Recover Coulomb’s Law. For a point charge, \(V = k_e q/r\), so

\[E_r = -\frac{dV}{dr} = -\frac{d}{dr}\left(k_e\frac{q}{r}\right) = k_e\frac{q}{r^2}\]

Coulomb’s Law walks back out. The potential formulation did not replace the field formulation — it stores the same content in one function instead of three, and differentiation is the key that unlocks it.

Reading the field without computing it

The gradient is a formula, but most of what it tells you can be had without evaluating anything. \(\vec{E} = -\nabla V\) says the field points downhill in potential, steepest-first. That is enough to answer a large class of questions from the behavior of \(V\) near a point, with no derivative taken.

The procedure is three steps:

  1. Establish whether \(V\) is rising or falling as you move through the point, and in which direction.
  2. The field points the way \(V\) falls fastest.
  3. A positive charge accelerates along \(\vec{E}\); a negative charge accelerates against it. Either way it moves toward lower potential energy \(qV\).

Direction from behavior alone

Suppose along the \(x\)-axis you know only three facts: \(V\) is positive a short distance to the left of point B, \(V = 0\) at B, and \(V \rightarrow -\infty\) some distance to the right of B, where a negative charge sits.

You have computed nothing. But \(V\) is decreasing left-to-right through B, so \(dV/dx < 0\) there, so \(E_x = -dV/dx\) is positive — the field at B points in \(+x\), toward the negative charge. A proton released at B accelerates in \(+x\); an electron released at B accelerates in \(-x\).

Why this is not a shortcut but the actual content. The magnitude of \(E\) at B requires the derivative. The direction does not — it requires only the sign of a slope, and a sign can be read off three sampled values, a sketch, or a physical argument about which charge dominates nearby.

Notice also that the argument never needed \(V\) at B to be zero. A zero of potential carries no information about the field; it was the slope through B that mattered, and a function can pass through zero with any slope at all. This is the §24.4 warning in its most useful form: do not reason from the value of \(V\), reason from how \(V\) changes.

Why bother with potential at all?

  1. Scalars add. Compare §24.4’s superposition against Chapter 22’s.
  2. Energy is immediate. \(\Delta U_E = q\Delta V\) — no integration once \(V\) is known.
  3. It is what instruments read. A voltmeter measures potential difference. There is no such thing as a field-meter you clip onto two points.
  4. Circuits are built on it. Every result in Chapters 26–27 is a statement about potential difference.

24.6 — Electric Potential Due to Continuous Charge Distributions

There are two routes to the potential of an extended distribution, and they are good for different things.

Route Use it when Section
\(V = k_e\displaystyle\int\frac{dq}{r}\) — sum contributions the geometry is simple and you have no field yet §24.6, below
\(\Delta V = -\displaystyle\int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}\) — integrate a known field Gauss’s Law already gave you \(\vec{E}\) §24.6, “the other route”

The first builds \(V\) from charge. The second builds \(V\) from a field you already did the work to find. Recognising which one is cheaper is most of the skill.

Route 1 — Summing Contributions

Chop the distribution into elements \(dq\), each contributing \(k_e\,dq/r\), and add:

\[\boxed{\;V = k_e\int\frac{dq}{r}\;}\]

Compare this with the corresponding field integral, which needs components and unit vectors. Here there is one scalar integrand and no directions to track — often the difference between a problem you can do and one you cannot.

Uniformly Charged Ring

Ring of radius \(a\), total charge \(Q\), field point P on the axis at distance \(x\).

Every element is the same distance from P, \(r = \sqrt{a^2+x^2}\). That constant comes straight out of the integral:

\[V = k_e\int\frac{dq}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}} = \frac{k_e}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}\int dq\]

\[\boxed{\;V = \frac{k_e Q}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}\;}\]

There was no integral to do. The geometry did the work — which is the payoff of choosing a distribution whose every element sits at one distance.

Get the field by differentiating.

\[E_x = -\frac{dV}{dx} = -\frac{d}{dx}\left(k_eQ\left(a^2+x^2\right)^{-1/2}\right) = \frac{k_eQx}{\left(a^2+x^2\right)^{3/2}}\]

This is exactly the ring field from Chapter 23, which took a vector setup, a symmetry argument to kill the perpendicular component, and an integral. Here it is one derivative of a result that required no integration at all.

Check the limits as before: at \(x=0\) the numerator vanishes, so \(E = 0\) at the center — but note \(V = k_eQ/a\) there, its maximum. The potential is largest exactly where the field is zero, because zero field means zero slope, and a smooth function with zero slope is at a turning point. For \(x \gg a\), \(E \rightarrow k_eQ/x^2\) and \(V \rightarrow k_eQ/x\): a point charge, as it must be.

Uniformly Charged Disk

Radius \(R\), uniform surface density \(\sigma\), field point on the axis at \(x\). Build the disk out of rings — each of radius \(r\) and thickness \(dr\) carries \(dq = \sigma\left(2\pi r\,dr\right)\) and we already know a ring’s potential:

\[V = \int_0^R \frac{k_e\left(2\pi\sigma r\,dr\right)}{\sqrt{r^2+x^2}} = 2\pi k_e\sigma\int_0^R\frac{r\,dr}{\sqrt{r^2+x^2}}\]

\[\boxed{\;V = 2\pi k_e\sigma\left(\sqrt{R^2+x^2}-x\right) = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\sqrt{R^2+x^2}-x\right)\;}\]

Note the method: the ring was not an end in itself. It was built to be the element of the disk, exactly as the disk will be the element of other things. This is the same escalation you used in Chapter 23.

The infinite-sheet limit. Let \(R \gg x\) — stand very close to a very large disk. Then \(\sqrt{R^2+x^2}\rightarrow R\), and

\[V \rightarrow \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(R - x\right)\]

so \(E_x = -dV/dx = \sigma/2\varepsilon_0\): constant, independent of distance, which is precisely the infinite-plane result from Gauss’s Law in §23.5. Two completely different routes — a flux argument and an axial integral — meeting at the same number is the strongest kind of check available.

Finite Line of Charge

A rod of length \(\ell\) carries \(Q\) uniformly, \(\lambda = Q/\ell\), lying along the \(x\)-axis from \(0\) to \(\ell\); P sits at height \(a\) above the near end.

\[V = k_e\lambda\int_0^\ell\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = k_e\lambda\Big[\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right)\Big]_0^\ell\]

\[\boxed{\;V = k_e\frac{Q}{\ell}\ln\left(\frac{\ell+\sqrt{\ell^2+a^2}}{a}\right)\;}\]

Far away, \(a \gg \ell\): expanding the logarithm gives \(V \approx k_eQ/a\) — a point charge again, as any bounded distribution must be from far enough off.

The logarithm is the signature of a line. You met it in Chapter 23 as the \(1/r\) field of a line charge; integrate \(1/r\) and you get \(\ln r\). Whenever a logarithm appears in an electrostatics answer, look for a one-dimensional source.

Route 2 — Integrating a Known Field

When Gauss’s Law has already handed you \(\vec{E}\), do not go back to the charge. Integrate the field you have:

\[V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}\]

This is the same relation used in §24.3, but nothing now requires \(\vec{E}\) to be uniform. Whatever position-dependence the field carries goes straight into the integral.

Warm-Up: A Field That Grows With Distance

Before the radial cases, take the simplest non-uniform field there is. A region contains \(\vec{E} = Cx\,\hat{i}\) with \(C = 400\ \text{N}/(\text{C}\cdot\text{m})\). Find \(\Delta V\) between \(x_a = 0.500\ \text{m}\) and \(x_b = 1.50\ \text{m}\), moving along the \(x\)-axis.

Along the axis \(d\vec{s} = dx\,\hat{i}\), so \(\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s} = \left(Cx\right)dx\) and the integral is a polynomial:

\[\Delta V = -\int_{x_a}^{x_b} Cx\,dx = -C\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{x_a}^{x_b}\]

\[\boxed{\;\Delta V = -\frac{C}{2}\left(x_b^{2} - x_a^{2}\right) = -400\ \text{V}\;}\]

Two checks, both cheap. The displacement is along \(\vec{E}\), so \(V\) must fall — and it does. And because \(E\) is linear in \(x\), its average across the interval equals its value at the midpoint: \(E(1.00\ \text{m}) = 400\) N/C, and a uniform \(400\ \text{N/C}\) over \(\Delta x = 1.00\) m gives \(-400\) V, exactly the integral’s answer.

That shortcut is not general. It worked only because \(E\) is linear; for the \(1/r\) fields below, the midpoint value is not the average and the trick fails. Knowing when a shortcut is licensed is worth more than the shortcut.

Between Two Coaxial Conductors

An inner conductor of radius \(a\) and a concentric outer shell of radius \(b\), both of length \(\ell\), carry \(+Q\) and \(-Q\). Find the potential difference between them.

Step 1 — get the field from Gauss’s Law. A coaxial cylindrical surface of radius \(r\), with \(a<r<b\) and length \(\ell\), encloses \(Q\). By cylindrical symmetry \(\vec{E}\) is radial and constant on that surface, and the end caps carry no flux:

\[E\left(2\pi r\ell\right) = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E(r) = \frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 \ell\, r} = \frac{2k_e\lambda}{r}\]

with \(\lambda = Q/\ell\). The field falls as \(1/r\) — the infinite-line result of §23.5, which is what a long coaxial cable looks like from inside the gap.

Step 2 — integrate it inward. Walk radially from \(b\) to \(a\), so \(d\vec{s} = dr\,\hat{r}\) and \(\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s} = E\,dr\):

\[V_a - V_b = -\int_b^a \frac{2k_e\lambda}{r}\,dr = 2k_e\lambda\int_a^b\frac{dr}{r}\]

\[\boxed{\;\Delta V = V_a - V_b = 2k_e\lambda\ln\!\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)\;}\]

Where the logarithm came from, and why it had to. Nothing was integrated by brute force — \(\int dr/r = \ln r\), and that is the only place a logarithm can enter. Trace it back: the log is here because the field went as \(1/r\), and the field went as \(1/r\) because the source is effectively one-dimensional.

Contrast a spherical geometry, where \(E \sim 1/r^2\) integrates to \(1/a - 1/b\) — a difference of reciprocals, no logarithm anywhere. The functional form of a potential difference is a fingerprint of the source’s dimensionality, and you can predict which form you will get before doing the integral.

Sign check. \(b>a\) makes \(\ln(b/a)>0\), so \(V_a > V_b\): the inner conductor, carrying the positive charge, sits at the higher potential. Correct — and note the check cost nothing but reading the sign of a logarithm.

Limiting case. As \(b \rightarrow a\) the gap closes, \(\ln(b/a)\rightarrow 0\), and \(\Delta V \rightarrow 0\). Two conductors pressed together cannot hold a potential difference, which is what a short circuit is.

Why this one matters. \(\Delta V\) is proportional to \(Q\) — double the charge and you double the potential difference, because \(\lambda\) appears linearly and the geometry factor \(\ln(b/a)\) does not care about charge at all. That fixed ratio \(Q/\Delta V\) depends only on the geometry, and in Chapter 25 it is given a name: capacitance.

24.7 — Potential of a Charged Conductor

A conductor is an equipotential

Chapter 23 established that \(\vec{E} = 0\) everywhere inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium. Combine that with \(\vec{E} = -\nabla V\): if the gradient is zero throughout a region, \(V\) is constant throughout it.

\[\boxed{\;\text{Every point on and inside a conductor in equilibrium is at the same potential.}\;}\]

This single sentence carries three of Chapter 23’s separate results:

  • The surface is an equipotential, so field lines meet it perpendicularly — Chapter 22’s rule 5, now derived rather than asserted.
  • Charge redistributes until the potential is uniform; that redistribution is the approach to equilibrium.
  • Two conductors connected by a wire become one conductor, hence one potential — which is why “ground” is a single number and why circuit nodes have voltages.

A Charged Conducting Sphere

Radius \(R\), total charge \(Q\):

Region \(V\) \(E\)
\(r \geq R\) \(k_eQ/r\) \(k_eQ/r^2\)
\(r \leq R\) \(k_eQ/R\) (constant) \(0\)

The two must agree at the surface, and they do: setting \(r = R\) in the outside expression gives \(k_eQ/R\), the inside value. \(V\) is continuous.

But \(E\) is not continuous — it jumps from \(0\) to \(k_eQ/R^2\) across the surface. There is no contradiction: \(E\) is the slope of \(V\), and a function can be continuous while its slope jumps. \(V(r)\) has a kink at \(r=R\) — flat inside, falling outside. The field discontinuity is the kink.

Sharp Points

On an irregular conductor, charge piles up where the curvature is high. High \(\sigma\) means high local field, \(E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0\) just outside — even though the whole surface sits at one potential. Potential is uniform; field is not.

  • Lightning rods exploit it: the intense field at the tip ionises air and gives the strike a preferred path.
  • Van de Graaff domes avoid it: smooth and large, to hold charge without leaking it into the air.
  • Corona discharge is the visible version — the glow at a sharp electrode.

24.8 — Assembling a Charge Distribution

§24.1 asked what the potential energy of an existing configuration is. This section asks what it cost to build — the same number, approached as a process, which is the view Chapter 25 needs for capacitors.

(For a charge already in place and set moving — released from rest, gaining speed as it falls through a potential difference — the tool is energy conservation, \(K_i + qV_i = K_f + qV_f\), developed in §24.3.)

Bring charges in one at a time from infinity. The first is free — there is no field yet to work against. The second costs \(q_2V_1\), where \(V_1\) is the first charge’s potential at the second’s destination. The third costs \(q_3\left(V_1+V_2\right)\), and so on:

\[U_E = \sum_i q_i V_i^{\,\text{(due to those already placed)}} = k_e\sum_{i<j}\frac{q_iq_j}{r_{ij}}\]

which recovers §24.1’s result — as it must, since potential energy depends on configuration and not on the order of assembly.

What a negative assembly cost actually looks like. The triangle in §24.1 came to \(U_E = -0.240\) J, so building it took \(W_{\text{ext}} = -0.240\) J — a sentence that is easy to accept and hard to picture. Picture it this way: you are not pushing those charges together, you are holding them back. They fall toward one another on their own, and your hand is the brake. The \(0.240\) J is not delivered into the configuration; it is extracted from it. A negative \(W_{\text{ext}}\) is not an absence of work — it is work done against the direction of motion. Flip \(q_3\) to \(+3.0\ \mu\text{C}\) and the sign flips with it: now \(W_{\text{ext}} = +0.480\) J, and you genuinely are pushing, against three mutual repulsions, every step of the way.

Order-independence is a real constraint, not an observation. If assembling in a different order gave a different total, \(U_E\) would not be a state function and the conservative-force argument of §24.1 would collapse. Try it on the triangle from §24.1: bring in \(q_3\) first instead of last, and the three pair terms arrive in a different sequence but sum to the same \(-0.240\) J.

Looking ahead: in Chapter 25 this same assembly cost, applied to charge piling up on capacitor plates, becomes \(U = Q^2/2C\) — and then gets reinterpreted once more as energy stored in the field itself, at a density \(u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\).

24.9 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Potential is potential energy per unit charge, \(V = U_E/q\) — a property of the space, not of what you put in it.
  2. Potential difference is the line integral of the field: \(\Delta V = -\int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}\).
  3. One volt is one joule per coulomb, and \(1\ \text{N/C} = 1\ \text{V/m}\) says the field is the rate of change of potential with position.
  4. Field lines point downhill in potential. Every charge moves so as to lower its own potential energy.
  5. Equipotentials are perpendicular to field lines, everywhere, and their spacing measures field strength.
  6. Potential superposes as a scalar — this is the chapter’s central advantage.
  7. \(V = 0\) does not imply \(E = 0\), and \(E = 0\) does not imply \(V = 0\).
  8. The field is recoverable, \(\vec{E} = -\nabla V\) — nothing was lost.
  9. A conductor in equilibrium is an equipotential, inside and on its surface.

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Potential energy, two point charges \(U_E = k_e\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r}\)
Potential energy, many charges \(U_E = k_e\sum_{i<j}\dfrac{q_iq_j}{r_{ij}}\)
Electric potential (definition) \(V = \dfrac{U_E}{q}\)
Potential difference \(\Delta V = -\displaystyle\int_A^B\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}\)
Uniform field \(\Delta V = -Ed\)
Point charge \(V = k_e\dfrac{q}{r}\)
Several point charges \(V = k_e\sum_i\dfrac{q_i}{r_i}\)
Continuous distribution \(V = k_e\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dq}{r}\)
Field from potential \(\vec{E} = -\nabla V\)
Between coaxial conductors \(\Delta V = 2k_e\lambda\ln\left(b/a\right)\)
Energy conservation \(K_i + qV_i = K_f + qV_f\)
Electron volt \(1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}\)

Connections to Physics I

Mechanics Electrostatics
Gravitational PE \(U_g = mgh\) Electric PE \(U_E = qV\)
Height \(h\) Potential \(V\)
Gravitational potential \(V_g = gh\) Electric potential \(V = U_E/q\)
\(\vec{g} = -\nabla V_g\) \(\vec{E} = -\nabla V\)

Looking Ahead

Chapter 25 takes the last idea of this chapter — that separating charge costs energy — and builds a device around it. A capacitor is two conductors, each an equipotential by §24.7, held at a potential difference. Its capacitance is

\[C = \frac{Q}{\Delta V}\]

and the energy you stored getting the charge there is \(U = \tfrac12 C\left(\Delta V\right)^2\). Chapter 25 then makes the move this chapter has been setting up: that energy is not really “in the charges” at all, but distributed through the field between the plates at a density \(u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\).

Coulomb’s Law, Gauss’s Law, and electric potential are three descriptions of one phenomenon — forces, fields, and energy. Each makes a different class of problem easy. Knowing which to reach for is the skill; it comes from having done all three.
